entries.outreach_draft:
Dear Universal Music Publishing,

We are writing on behalf of the production 'Street Orchestra Flash Mob' to request a synchronisation licence and a master use licence for the musical work 'My Love'.

The material appears from 0:00:00 to 0:01:00, for an approximate duration of one minute. The scene depicts an instrumental street performance by a philharmonic orchestra, including flute, violins, cello, guitar, and percussion, of the song 'My Love'. This use is prominent.

We are seeking rights for worldwide, all media, in perpetuity.

Please note that the composition and the sound recording may be controlled separately. If you control only one side, please advise.

We require guidance on the current ownership of the musical work and any associated sound recording. The supplied description indicates an instrumental philharmonic performance, while our research points to Westlife's 2000 recording. Please confirm whether the cut uses the Westlife master or a newly recorded orchestra master. If a new master recording is used, please identify the orchestra, producer, recording owner, arranger, and provide performer releases. We also seek clarification on composition-side shares and current publishers or administrators for Per Magnusson, David Kreuger, and Pelle Nylén, as these were not identified in our reviewed public records. Please provide title-specific PRO/CMO repertoire records, IPI/ISWC data, and publisher confirmations.

Please confirm if you are able to grant these rights, your fee, and any restrictions that may apply.

Information Designed to comfortably sit side-by-side with musical notation, Rhapsody’s eccentric, nostalgic structure finds its footing from an unusual place. Born out of research from Reading University which discovered that the design of contemporary musical notation was inspired by the typographical structure and rationale of the classic typeface, Didot, Rhapsody emerged. item.title: ALDO
item.description: The logo for the shoe and accessory brand 'ALDO' is visible on a storefront sign on a building in the background.
item.evidence: The white text 'ALDO' is clearly legible on the building behind the performers.

holders.name: The Aldo Group Inc. / Le Groupe Aldo Inc.
holders.territory: United States confirmed; worldwide ownership and control not fully verified
holders.contact: Media: media@aldogroup.com. Website and general corporate inquiries: Aldoweb@aldogroup.com or corpcustomer@aldogroup.com.
holders.notes: ALDO's official terms identify The Aldo Group Inc. as the owner of the registered ALDO word mark and ALDO logo. The published materials do not identify a dedicated film/television clearance desk; request written trademark and brand-use approval through the corporate or media contacts and ask that the matter be routed to legal/brand licensing.

finding.public_domain_rationale: The material is a trademark and logo, not a copyright work that can be treated as public domain. ALDO's official terms state that ALDO and the ALDO logo are registered trademarks of The Aldo Group Inc. and may not be copied or used without the applicable trademark holder's written permission. The requested recognizable background storefront depiction should therefore be treated as requiring clearance, particularly because it is intended for worldwide commercial exploitation in all media in perpetuity.
finding.territory_notes: The ALDO word mark is confirmed as live and registered in the United States (U.S. Registration No. 2,826,814). Trademark protection is territorial, so a worldwide, all-media license should be cleared for each relevant country; the U.S. record alone does not establish worldwide coverage or identify local licensees.
finding.licensing_precedent: No publicly documented ALDO placement in a third-party film or television production, or ALDO-specific placement fee, was identified. General industry references report placements ranging from free loan/trade arrangements to approximately US$50,000–US$500,000, with million-dollar film placements described as uncommon or at the high end; these are not ALDO-specific quotes.
unresolved: No dedicated ALDO entertainment-clearance department or named approval executive is publicly identified; the published contacts are general corporate, website, and media contacts.
The current ownership and licensing status of the ALDO word mark and logo in every territory covered by the requested worldwide license has not been verified from the available records.
No written ALDO approval, fee quote, or license terms were located for the specific film, background storefront depiction, worldwide territory, all-media use, or perpetual term.

basis.reasoning: The official ALDO terms identify the ALDO name and logo as registered trademarks and state that they may not be copied or used without written permission. That directly supports treating the depicted mark as protected rather than public-domain material.

item.title: Highlands Coffee
item.description: The logo for the 'Highlands Coffee' chain is visible on a large, circular sign on the main building in the background.
item.evidence: The distinctive red and green logo and partial text are visible on the curved building facade.

holders.name: Highlands Coffee Service Joint Stock Company
holders.notes: The official application terms identify this company as Highlands Coffee and state that the marks are owned or controlled by it or licensed to it. This is the primary clearance contact for a film or television request, although no dedicated entertainment-licensing function is published.

holders.name: SuperFoods Group
holders.contact: Use the Highlands Coffee contact supplied by Jollibee Group: customerservice@highlandscoffee.com.vn
holders.notes: Jollibee Group states that SuperFoods Group owns Highlands Coffee. The available material does not identify SuperFoods Group's exact legal entity or prove that it is the registered owner of the specific logo shown.

holders.name: Jollibee Foods Corporation
holders.contact: Jollibee Group directs Highlands Coffee enquiries to customerservice@highlandscoffee.com.vn
holders.notes: Jollibee states that it owns 60% of SuperFoods Group, which owns Highlands Coffee. This supports an indirect controlling interest, not necessarily direct ownership of the depicted trademark.

holders.name: Viet Thai International Joint Stock Company
holders.notes: Public descriptions identify Highlands Coffee as a registered brand of Viet Thai International and describe SuperFoods Group as a joint venture involving Viet Thai. The precise present-day trademark interest and share require documentary confirmation.

finding.public_domain_rationale: A trademark and logo are not works that become freely usable merely because the brand was introduced in 1999. The official Highlands Coffee site states that the brand was established in 1999, while the official terms state that the marks are owned or controlled by Highlands Coffee or licensed to it and that rights not expressly granted are reserved. The proposed use therefore requires trademark clearance rather than a public-domain analysis.
finding.territory_notes: The trademark is not public-domain material. The available evidence identifies Vietnamese ownership and operation, but does not establish worldwide trademark ownership, territorial registrations, or any international licensing representative. For the proposed worldwide use, obtain approval covering each relevant territory and media category.
finding.licensing_precedent: No publicly documented film or television licence, entertainment depiction approval, or reported licence fee for the Highlands Coffee trademark was located. The published policy is not entertainment-specific: the application terms limit the stated user licence to personal use and reserve all other rights.
unresolved: The specific trademark-registration certificates, registration numbers, classes, and current registrants for the depicted red-and-green logo were not located.

The relationship between SuperFoods Group, Highlands Coffee Service Joint Stock Company, and Viet Thai International Joint Stock Company is not fully documented in the available public records for trademark-clearance purposes.
No dedicated film-and-television licensing department or representative was identified; the available contact is general customer service.
No written approval, release, or trademark licence for Street Orchestra Flash Mob has been documented.
The applicable rights and approval authority outside Vietnam remain unconfirmed.

basis.reasoning: The official terms classify the logos and marks as proprietary marks owned or controlled by Highlands Coffee or licensed to it, grant only a limited personal-use application licence, and reserve all other rights. That supports a negative public-domain determination for the trademark/logo.

citations.title: About Peavey
excerpts: For over six decades, Peavey has blazed its own path toward musical perfection. Founded by Hartley Peavey in 1965 as a one-man shop, today Peavey Electronics Corporation is one of the largest makers and suppliers of musical instruments, amplifiers and professional audio systems in the world—distributing more than 2,000 products to more than 130 countries. Hartley has famously said, "In order to be better, by definition you must be different." What makes Peavey different is a commitment to approaching business with a unique vision, from product design to distribution to being the largest independently owned manufacturer in the business. His quest has led to more than 180 patents and innovations in the way we hear and play music. Hartley Peavey is not only the founder, visionary and catalyst, but also the lynchpin that connects a rich history to a bright future. excerpts: An Innovator Emerges Hartley Peavey inherits his first set of hand tools from his grandfather, J.L. Peavey, and becomes the youngest person to enroll in Ross Collins Vocational School in Meridian. Hartley's skills advance quickly as he learns how to use lathes and millings machines. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1957.png) 1957 Hartley Builds His First Amplifier Hartley works in his father's music store, Peavey's Melody Music in Meridian, which is frequented by rock & roll, country and R&B pioneers. Inspired by a Bo Diddley concert, Hartley Peavey decides to become a rock & roll guitar player. After converting his acoustic guitar to an electric, he builds the first Peavey amplifier. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1958.jpg) 1958 Hartley's Creativity Flows Hartley Peavey sketches his first guitar design in high school—and it bears more than a passing resemblance to the future Peavey Mystic guitar, complete with the trademark headstock scoop that will later distinguish many Peavey guitars. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1959.jpg) 1959 Lightning—and Inspiration—Strike During his senior year of high school, Hartley designs his future company's lightning-bolt logo. "I wanted to have a very distinctive logo," said Hartley. "So I came up with the concept where the 'P' and 'V,' and the 'A' and 'Y,' would more or less intersect." Today, this logo is instantly recognizable all over the world. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1961.jpg) 1961 The Brand is Born Hartley builds the first Peavey-branded amplifier, complete with rudimentary "lightning bolt" logo, in the basement of the Peavey family home. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1964.png) 1964 The First Patent The U.S. Patent Office issues Hartley's first patent (No. 3,151,699) for an early Peavey amplifier design. To date, Peavey has earned more than 180 patents in music and audio. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1965.png) 1965 Hartley Peavey Establishes Peavey Electronics Corporation Hartley establishes Peavey Electronics Corporation in the loft above Peavey's Melody Music in Meridian, Mississippi. In a time of mass conglomeration, buyouts and price hikes, Hartley establishes a new niche in music and audio equipment, providing "quality gear at a fair price." Production begins on the Peavey Musician™ and Dyna-Bass™ amplifiers, hand-built at a rate of one unit per week. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1967.png) 1967 Hartley Hires His First Salesman When an unsuspecting traveling amplifier salesman challenged Hartley to a shootout with his wares at Peavey's Melody Music, Hartley dutifully wheeled in one of his new amps and blew away his competition. The salesman left without saying a word, but his colleague soon returned and asked to be Hartley's salesman. "I can't afford to pay you," Hartley insisted. But that didn't phase Don Belfield.

citations.title: About Peavey
excerpts: For over six decades, Peavey has blazed its own path toward musical perfection. Founded by Hartley Peavey in 1965 as a one-man shop, today Peavey Electronics Corporation is one of the largest makers and suppliers of musical instruments, amplifiers and professional audio systems in the world—distributing more than 2,000 products to more than 130 countries. Hartley has famously said, "In order to be better, by definition you must be different." What makes Peavey different is a commitment to approaching business with a unique vision, from product design to distribution to being the largest independently owned manufacturer in the business. His quest has led to more than 180 patents and innovations in the way we hear and play music. Hartley Peavey is not only the founder, visionary and catalyst, but also the lynchpin that connects a rich history to a bright future. And his founding principles of quality, reliability and innovation are still the focus of engineering and manufacturing operations that span continents and languages, customs and cultures. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Distribution.svg) Distribution 130+ Countries ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Patents.svg) Patents 180+ Worldwide ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Catalog.svg) Catalog 2,000+ Products Founded 1965 Headquarters Meridian, MS, USA Founder and Chairman Hartley D.

citations.title: About Peavey
excerpts: An Innovator Emerges Hartley Peavey inherits his first set of hand tools from his grandfather, J.L. Peavey, and becomes the youngest person to enroll in Ross Collins Vocational School in Meridian. Hartley's skills advance quickly as he learns how to use lathes and millings machines. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1957.png) 1957 Hartley Builds His First Amplifier Hartley works in his father's music store, Peavey's Melody Music in Meridian, which is frequented by rock & roll, country and R&B pioneers. Inspired by a Bo Diddley concert, Hartley Peavey decides to become a rock & roll guitar player. After converting his acoustic guitar to an electric, he builds the first Peavey amplifier. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1958.jpg) 1958 Hartley's Creativity Flows Hartley Peavey sketches his first guitar design in high school—and it bears more than a passing resemblance to the future Peavey Mystic guitar, complete with the trademark headstock scoop that will later distinguish many Peavey guitars. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1959.jpg) 1959 Lightning—and Inspiration—Strike During his senior year of high school, Hartley designs his future company's lightning-bolt logo. "I wanted to have a very distinctive logo," said Hartley. "So I came up with the concept where the 'P' and 'V,' and the 'A' and 'Y,' would more or less intersect." Today, this logo is instantly recognizable all over the world. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1961.jpg) 1961 The Brand is Born Hartley builds the first Peavey-branded amplifier, complete with rudimentary "lightning bolt" logo, in the basement of the Peavey family home. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1964.png) 1964 The First Patent The U.S. Patent Office issues Hartley's first patent (No. 3,151,699) for an early Peavey amplifier design. To date, Peavey has earned more than 180 patents in music and audio. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1965.png) 1965 Hartley Peavey Establishes Peavey Electronics Corporation Hartley establishes Peavey Electronics Corporation in the loft above Peavey's Melody Music in Meridian, Mississippi. In a time of mass conglomeration, buyouts and price hikes, Hartley establishes a new niche in music and audio equipment, providing "quality gear at a fair price." Production begins on the Peavey Musician™ and Dyna-Bass™ amplifiers, hand-built at a rate of one unit per week. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1967.png) 1967 Hartley Hires His First Salesman When an unsuspecting traveling amplifier salesman challenged Hartley to a shootout with his wares at Peavey's Melody Music, Hartley dutifully wheeled in one of his new amps and blew away his competition. The salesman left without saying a word, but his colleague soon returned and asked to be Hartley's salesman. "I can't afford to pay you," Hartley insisted. But that didn't phase Don Belfield. He convinced Hartley to give him the amp to sell, which he did—quickly. Belfield became an integral part of the company's early success. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1968.jpg) 1968 Peavey Enters Sound Reinforcement Market Peavey diversifies into P.A. systems with the successful PA-3™, the first affordable sound system of its kind, allowing countless musicians to take their talents from the garage to the stage. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1968a.jpg) 1968 Peavey Opens First Factory Peavey leaves behind the loft space and moves into Plant 1, the first standalone Peavey factory. The building measured 100 feet by 32 feet, but eventually expanded to overtake the entire city block. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1969.jpg) 1969 The Silver Stripe The Peavey "silver stripe" trademark design is born when Hartley puts the grille frame onto a speaker cabinet backwards, with the aluminum mounting extrusions on the outside. He likes the look so much it becomes the company's signature design aesthetic for the next 25 years. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1970.jpg) 1970 First Stop: Nashville Country music embraces the Peavey philosophy of "quality gear at a fair price." The Peavey artist roster soon includes stars like Merle Haggard, Hank Williams Jr., Mel Tillis, Dr. Hook & the Medicine Show, the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band and the Grand Ole Opry. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1972.jpg) 1972 Unprecedented Growth

citations.title: About Peavey
excerpts: An Innovator Emerges Hartley Peavey inherits his first set of hand tools from his grandfather, J.L. Peavey, and becomes the youngest person to enroll in Ross Collins Vocational School in Meridian. Hartley's skills advance quickly as he learns how to use lathes and millings machines. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1957.png) 1957 Hartley Builds His First Amplifier Hartley works in his father's music store, Peavey's Melody Music in Meridian, which is frequented by rock & roll, country and R&B pioneers. Inspired by a Bo Diddley concert, Hartley Peavey decides to become a rock & roll guitar player. After converting his acoustic guitar to an electric, he builds the first Peavey amplifier. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1958.jpg) 1958 Hartley's Creativity Flows Hartley Peavey sketches his first guitar design in high school—and it bears more than a passing resemblance to the future Peavey Mystic guitar, complete with the trademark headstock scoop that will later distinguish many Peavey guitars. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1959.jpg) 1959 Lightning—and Inspiration—Strike During his senior year of high school, Hartley designs his future company's lightning-bolt logo. "I wanted to have a very distinctive logo," said Hartley. "So I came up with the concept where the 'P' and 'V,' and the 'A' and 'Y,' would more or less intersect." Today, this logo is instantly recognizable all over the world. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1961.jpg) 1961 The Brand is Born Hartley builds the first Peavey-branded amplifier, complete with rudimentary "lightning bolt" logo, in the basement of the Peavey family home. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1964.png) 1964 The First Patent The U.S. Patent Office issues Hartley's first patent (No. 3,151,699) for an early Peavey amplifier design. To date, Peavey has earned more than 180 patents in music and audio. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1965.png) 1965 Hartley Peavey Establishes Peavey Electronics Corporation Hartley establishes Peavey Electronics Corporation in the loft above Peavey's Melody Music in Meridian, Mississippi. In a time of mass conglomeration, buyouts and price hikes, Hartley establishes a new niche in music and audio equipment, providing "quality gear at a fair price." Production begins on the Peavey Musician™ and Dyna-Bass™ amplifiers, hand-built at a rate of one unit per week. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1967.png) 1967 Hartley Hires His First Salesman When an unsuspecting traveling amplifier salesman challenged Hartley to a shootout with his wares at Peavey's Melody Music, Hartley dutifully wheeled in one of his new amps and blew away his competition. The salesman left without saying a word, but his colleague soon returned and asked to be Hartley's salesman. "I can't afford to pay you," Hartley insisted. But that didn't phase Don Belfield. He convinced Hartley to give him the amp to sell, which he did—quickly. Belfield became an integral part of the company's early success. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1968.jpg) 1968 Peavey Enters Sound Reinforcement Market Peavey diversifies into P.A. systems with the successful PA-3™, the first affordable sound system of its kind, allowing countless musicians to take their talents from the garage to the stage. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1968a.jpg) 1968 Peavey Opens First Factory Peavey leaves behind the loft space and moves into Plant 1, the first standalone Peavey factory. The building measured 100 feet by 32 feet, but eventually expanded to overtake the entire city block. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1969.jpg) 1969 The Silver Stripe The Peavey "silver stripe" trademark design is born when Hartley puts the grille frame onto a speaker cabinet backwards, with the aluminum mounting extrusions on the outside. He likes the look so much it becomes the company's signature design aesthetic for the next 25 years. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1970.jpg) 1970 First Stop: Nashville Country music embraces the Peavey philosophy of "quality gear at a fair price." The Peavey artist roster soon includes stars like Merle Haggard, Hank Williams Jr., Mel Tillis, Dr. Hook & the Medicine Show, the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band and the Grand Ole Opry. ![](https://peavey.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/1972.jpg) 1972 Unprecedented Growth

item.title: Hoan Kiem Lake Plaza, Hanoi
item.description: A distinctive public square featuring a large, multi-story circular building (the 'Ham Ca Map' building), a fountain, and heavy pedestrian and scooter traffic.
item.evidence: The unique architecture of the circular building is a well-known landmark.

holders.name: Hanoi People's Committee
holders.notes: The city reportedly leased the site to Transerco and is the relevant public-land authority. The available record does not prove whether the city or Transerco held title to the building improvements.

holders.name: Hanoi Transport Corporation (Transerco)
holders.notes: Reported manager and operator of the Ham Ca Map building, following the merger of the Hanoi Tram Enterprise into Transerco. Contact for any historical building, tenant, or location-release records.

holders.name: Vietnam Cinema Department, Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism
holders.notes: Permit authority for film production in Vietnam, particularly relevant if the production involved foreign personnel or commercial filming in Vietnam. This is a regulatory authority rather than a demonstrated title holder.

finding.public_domain_rationale: The building was constructed/completed around 1991–1993, placing its architectural design after the 1 December 1990 threshold for U.S. architectural-work protection. U.S. guidance treats the building design as an architectural work and generally applies life-plus-70 or work-made-for-hire terms; no evidence shows that the design term has expired. Accordingly, the architectural design should not be treated as public domain. Separately, 17 U.S.C. §120(a) permits pictorial representations of a constructed building located in or ordinarily visible from a public place, so an exterior background shot may not require architectural-copyright permission in the United States even though the design itself is not public domain.
finding.territory_notes: The Ham Ca Map building was demolished beginning 19 June 2025, so the production's shot is necessarily historical or archival rather than a current filming opportunity. For U.S. copyright purposes, an exterior architectural work ordinarily visible from a public place may be photographed or filmed under 17 U.S.C. §120(a), but that statutory exception does not resolve Vietnamese location permissions, traffic/public-space controls, trademark issues, or rights in the production's underlying footage. The Hoan Kiem Lake area is a specially protected national historical site. No site-specific published filming-permission policy for Ham Ca Map or Hoan Kiem Lake Plaza was identified; commercial filming in Vietnam generally requires national and local approvals.
finding.licensing_precedent: No documented prior film or television licence, location release, or reported fee specific to Ham Ca Map or Hoan Kiem Lake Plaza was identified. Published Vietnam production guidance gives indicative permit-related ranges of approximately USD 200–800 for cultural sites and USD 300–1,500 for historical sites; these are market guidance, not a confirmed fee for this location.
unresolved: The public record identifies the Hanoi People's Committee as the city lessor and Hanoi Transport Corporation (Transerco) as the manager/operator, but does not establish through a deed, asset register, or lease the precise title holder of the building itself.

The copyright claimant for the architectural design has not been confirmed. The architect, any employer/work-for-hire arrangement, assignments, and the architect's date of death or any applicable corporate term remain undocumented.
A signed historical location release and any filming or public-space permit issued before the 19 June 2025 demolition have not been identified.
No specific trademark-registration result for “Ham Ca Map,” “Hàm Cá Mập,” or “City View” was identified; a formal trademark search and clearance remain outstanding.

basis.reasoning: The architectural-work guidance states that architectural works created on or after 1 December 1990 are copyrightable, while §120(a) separately permits pictorial representations of a constructed building visible from a public place. The building's 1990s date therefore supports “no” for public-domain status, while recognizing the separate U.S. filming exception.

Copyright protects architec- tural works created on or after December 1, 1990. Copyright also protects unconstructed architectural works embodied in unpublished plans or drawings on December 1, 1990, if the design was constructed on or before December 31, 2002. ... in an architectural work if the work is a humanly habitable structure that is intended to be both permanent and station- ary. Examples of works that satisfy this requirement include houses, office buildings, churches, and museums.

citations.title: Film Permits in Vietnam: A Step-by-Step Guide for Filmmakers | Fixers in Vietnam Blog
excerpts: Navigating Film Permits in Vietnam: Your Step-by-Step Guide Filming in Vietnam has unrivaled opportunities for unique imagery and engaging stories. Like many countries, Vietnam has its own regulations regarding film production, particularly for foreign crews. It is important to remember that film permits are not just a means of fulfilling Vietnamese law to allow for filming, but a vital step to ensure that you have a successful, safe and enjoyable shoot. ... Why Are Film Permits Important? Obtaining film permits is necessary for a number of reasons. First, permits demonstrate that the filmmaker is complying with Vietnamese regulations and laws regarding filming, therefore, protecting the filmmaker from crippling delays, fines or even the possibility of being deported! Second, permits will open doors to locations and other relevant businesses (especially if you are going to be filming on private property or at an event that requires official approval from local authorities or property owners). ... The Film Permitting Process The film permitting process usually involves a few key steps: Initial Discussion: Discuss your project’s outline, any locations you are considering, and your calendar with a local fixer or production company. Preparation of Documents: After your discussion with your fixer or production company, you will be required to submit several documents, with documents often being; detailed synopsis, script (translated into Vietnamese), crew-list, equipment list and letters of intent. Submitting for Approval: Your document package and application will be submitted to the Ministry of Culture, Sport and Tourism and all other relevant ministries (e.g. for sensitive topics film, the Ministry of Public Security) and local People's Committees. • Review and Approval: The authorities review your application and this may include some clarification and/or amendments to your production plan. Permit Issuance: Once approved, official permits are issued allowing your production to begin. What Documents do I need for Film Permits? Although specific requirements can differ, typical film permit documents commonly required include: Detailed synopsis and film script (To be translated into Vietnamese). List of your crew members with passport and roles. List of equipment for import. Filming schedule and filming locations. Letters of support or invitation from local partners. Proof of production company registration and insurance. How Long Does it Take to Get Film Permit Approval? Typically, for standard productions, film permit application will take from 2 to 4 weeks to be processed. For complex projects involving sensitive topics, several provinces, or extended historical/cultural sites it may take 4 to 6 weeks or longer. Speeding up the Permits may also incur added cost and is not guaranteed even if urgent processing is requested. ... What is a Fixer? We will make sure your application is legible and complete, giving your application maximum chance of timely approval and minimum delays. Our strong understanding of local nuances, regulations, and prior relationships with government bodies ensure that we smooth the process, with as little friction as possible. What are the Common Challenges and how to avoid them? The constant challenges that local productions in Vietnam face while filming include acquiring film permits under various language barriers, unforeseen bureaucratic issues and a misunderstanding of culture which can lead to film permit delays. ... Conclusion Gaining all your necessary film permits and permissions to film in Vietnam is an essential building block to successfully complete your production. The process must be undertaken with care and attention to detail and local regulations, but it is easily managed with local knowledge and support.

To whom it may concern,

I am writing on behalf of the production "Street Orchestra Flash Mob" to request permission for the use of footage filmed at Hoan Kiem Lake Plaza in Hanoi.

We are seeking worldwide rights for all media, in perpetuity.

We understand the Hanoi People's Committee is the city lessor and Hanoi Transport Corporation (Transerco) is the manager/operator. We would appreciate any guidance you can offer regarding the current ownership and copyright status of these elements.

Please confirm if you are the appropriate party to grant permission for this use. We would also appreciate information regarding any associated fees or restrictions.

item.title: Ray-Ban
item.description: The flutist wears a pair of Wayfarer-style sunglasses with the 'Ray-Ban' logo visible on the right lens.
item.evidence: A close-up shot shows the white script logo on the corner of the sunglasses lens.

holders.name: Luxottica Group S.p.A.
holders.territory: Worldwide brand ownership; trademark rights remain country-specific
holders.notes: Ray-Ban's official copyright information identifies its trademarks and logos as trademarks or registered trademarks of Luxottica Group S.p.A. in the U.S. and other countries. The published legal email is an IP-enforcement contact, not expressly an entertainment-licensing desk.

holders.name: Luxottica of America Inc.
holders.territory: United States administrative and operating contact
holders.contact: Ray-Ban.com Legal Department; OnlineIPenforcement@luxottica.com; 4000 Luxottica Place, Mason, Ohio 45040
holders.notes: The U.S. Ray-Ban terms identify Luxottica of America Inc. as the contracting entity and describe Luxottica as the owner of Ray-Ban for the website. Route a U.S. brand-use request here, but obtain confirmation that it has authority to approve worldwide film and television use.

finding.public_domain_rationale: This is a trademark-clearance issue, not a public-domain copyright license. Ray-Ban's official materials call the Ray-Ban name, logos and product identifiers proprietary trademarks of Luxottica and prohibit use without express written permission. The U.S. record identifies RAY-BAN as registered, with registration in 1978 and first use in commerce in 1937. Trademark protection is not extinguished merely because the mark is old or has been used for decades.
finding.territory_notes: Ray-Ban trademarks are identified as protected in the United States and other countries. The public materials do not disclose a country-by-country ownership split or grant a worldwide film/television license. citations.title: Rights clearance: A guide for independent filmmakers - 3 Rights assessed during clearance
excerpts: For companies and businesses, trademarks are an important way to communicate, attract and maintain consumers. Trademarks also are an important tool in preventing unfair competition between companies competing in the market. Producers should be reminded of the different aspects to better understand how the use of trademarks and designs in the project could impact third-party rights and why a rightsholder might oppose their use. The protection of trademarks is territorial and depends on registration (with very few exceptions). In other words, legal protection is a result of a registration, which is done on a territory-by-territory basis. Generally, trademarks are protected against confusion that other signs could generate in the consumer of that product or service. It is also protected against genericization and tarnishing (especially famous trademarks) where any form of use or depiction that could be detrimental would not be allowed. Trademarks also represent an asset that receives considerable investment from companies on the trademark likeness (or even the “aura” of the trademark), in particular luxury brands. Right owners normally try to exercise control over the use of their trademarks. In some cases, it might be understood that the use could be beneficial and they might even be willing to pay for the exposure (the best example of this is product placement deals). In other cases, the context of the use in the audiovisual project might lead to tarnishing or even the association of the brand with other products or services. Many financing agents, such as television channels and streaming platforms, have established policies on the use of trademarks (including product placement). Those policies, usually communicated to the producer beforehand, deal with precautions in including a trademark in the project, because trademarks are aimed at a defined group of consumers of the product or service identified by the mark. The expectations of the film are normally broader than the consumers of that trademark so there is a need to ensure that the trademark is used in the normal and expected way the product or service is consumed. For example, a brand of office tools to be used in an office environment and not to hurt a character of the film. The decision to obtain a license will be taken depending on the trademark, product and services and the use in the project. Any use without written authorization should be done in an appropriate context that is relevant to the product or service that it represents and where the use is minimized and does not take a central role in the scene (story point). Guidance on the use of real trademarks normally states that the products or services should be shown as originally designed and no comments are made endorsing or referring to the quality or characteristics of the trademark. For this reason, when producers need to show alcoholic beverages and tobacco products, they often decide to create fictional brands and props to avoid showing real brands.

excerpts: Designs Industrial design is a type of IP that protects ornamental or aesthetic aspects. If the materials were not created specifically for the project, an analysis of the protection over those materials start with the copyright status of those materials. citations.title: Rights clearance: A guide for independent filmmakers - 3 Rights assessed during clearance
excerpts: For companies and businesses, trademarks are an important way to communicate, attract and maintain consumers. Trademarks also are an important tool in preventing unfair competition between companies competing in the market. Producers should be reminded of the different aspects to better understand how the use of trademarks and designs in the project could impact third-party rights and why a rightsholder might oppose their use. The protection of trademarks is territorial and depends on registration (with very few exceptions). In other words, legal protection is a result of a registration, which is done on a territory-by-territory basis. Generally, trademarks are protected against confusion that other signs could generate in the consumer of that product or service. It is also protected against genericization and tarnishing (especially famous trademarks) where any form of use or depiction that could be detrimental would not be allowed. Trademarks also represent an asset that receives considerable investment from companies on the trademark likeness (or even the “aura” of the trademark), in particular luxury brands. Right owners normally try to exercise control over the use of their trademarks. In some cases, it might be understood that the use could be beneficial and they might even be willing to pay for the exposure (the best example of this is product placement deals). In other cases, the context of the use in the audiovisual project might lead to tarnishing or even the association of the brand with other products or services. Many financing agents, such as television channels and streaming platforms, have established policies on the use of trademarks (including product placement). Those policies, usually communicated to the producer beforehand, deal with precautions in including a trademark in the project, because trademarks are aimed at a defined group of consumers of the product or service identified by the mark. The expectations of the film are normally broader than the consumers of that trademark so there is a need to ensure that the trademark is used in the normal and expected way the product or service is consumed. For example, a brand of office tools to be used in an office environment and not to hurt a character of the film. The decision to obtain a license will be taken depending on the trademark, product and services and the use in the project. Any use without written authorization should be done in an appropriate context that is relevant to the product or service that it represents and where the use is minimized and does not take a central role in the scene (story point). Guidance on the use of real trademarks normally states that the products or services should be shown as originally designed and no comments are made endorsing or referring to the quality or characteristics of the trademark. For this reason, when producers need to show alcoholic beverages and tobacco products, they often decide to create fictional brands and props to avoid showing real brands.

In it, an examining attorney lists any legal problems with your chosen trademark, as well as with the application... Post-Registration FAQs Trademark FAQs Read frequently asked questions we receive from our customers. Keeping your registration alive Once you own a trademark registration, you must do a few important things to maintain that registration and keep it alive. First, you must use your trademark in commerce. Additionally, you must file certain documents at regular intervals to show that you're continuing to use your trademark. If you don't file these documents before the deadline, your registration will be canceled or will expire, or your extension of protection to the U.S. will be invalidated (if you filed via WIPO under the Madrid system). Exceptions to the requirement to use your trademark are rare. TEAS maintenance forms For more information, see the following: Continue using your trademark to maintain your registration Deadlines for filing registration maintenance documents Deadlines for registrations based on the Madrid Protocol Common mistakes to avoid What happens next and timelines Look out for misleading notices from private companies Questions Continue using your trademark to maintain your registration Generally, trademark owners are only entitled to a federal registration if they're using their trademark in commerce. That's why most applicants submit specimens when they apply — to show that they're using their trademark. However, demonstrating trademark use once isn't enough. You must regularly demonstrate use throughout the life of your trademark if you want to maintain your registration and keep its benefits. Process overview for required maintenance documents Typically, when you file a required maintenance document , you'll submit a signed declaration saying that you're continuing to use your trademark with the goods and services in your registration. You'll also submit one specimen for each class of goods or services.

citations.title: Rights clearance: A guide for independent filmmakers - 3 Rights assessed during clearance
excerpts: Trademarks and designs Trademarks From a purely legal point of view, trademarks are symbols (images and/or text) that are registered to identify a group of products or services. In a broader sense, they are an important element for the public to distinguish between different offerings. For companies and businesses, trademarks are an important way to communicate, attract and maintain consumers. Trademarks also are an important tool in preventing unfair competition between companies competing in the market. Producers should be reminded of the different aspects to better understand how the use of trademarks and designs in the project could impact third-party rights and why a rightsholder might oppose their use. The protection of trademarks is territorial and depends on registration (with very few exceptions). In other words, legal protection is a result of a registration, which is done on a territory-by-territory basis. Generally, trademarks are protected against confusion that other signs could generate in the consumer of that product or service. It is also protected against genericization and tarnishing (especially famous trademarks) where any form of use or depiction that could be detrimental would not be allowed. Trademarks also represent an asset that receives considerable investment from companies on the trademark likeness (or even the “aura” of the trademark), in particular luxury brands. Right owners normally try to exercise control over the use of their trademarks. In some cases, it might be understood that the use could be beneficial and they might even be willing to pay for the exposure (the best example of this is product placement deals). In other cases, the context of the use in the audiovisual project might lead to tarnishing or even the association of the brand with other products or services. Many financing agents, such as television channels and streaming platforms, have established policies on the use of trademarks (including product placement). Those policies, usually communicated to the producer beforehand, deal with precautions in including a trademark in the project, because trademarks are aimed at a defined group of consumers of the product or service identified by the mark. The expectations of the film are normally broader than the consumers of that trademark so there is a need to ensure that the trademark is used in the normal and expected way the product or service is consumed. For example, a brand of office tools to be used in an office environment and not to hurt a character of the film. The decision to obtain a license will be taken depending on the trademark, product and services and the use in the project. Any use without written authorization should be done in an appropriate context that is relevant to the product or service that it represents and where the use is minimized and does not take a central role in the scene (story point). Guidance on the use of real trademarks normally states that the products or services should be shown as originally designed and no comments are made endorsing or referring to the quality or characteristics of the trademark. For this reason, when producers need to show alcoholic beverages and tobacco products, they often decide to create fictional brands and props to avoid showing real brands.

entries.outreach_draft:
Dear Lulu Guinness,

We are writing on behalf of the production 'Street Orchestra Flash Mob' to request permission to use an artwork.

The artwork appears at timecode 0:00:11-0:00:12, for approximately 1 second. In the scene, a female violinist wears a grey sweater featuring a repeating pattern of red lips.

We are seeking worldwide, all media rights, in perpetuity, for the reproduction of this artwork.

We understand that the repeating red lips pattern is associated with Lulu Guinness. However, we do not have a still, garment label, production metadata, or an indexed production page that definitively ties the garment in 'Street Orchestra Flash Mob' to Lulu Guinness. Markus Lupfer is an alternative retail lead we are also considering. Regarding authorship, while the official Lulu Guinness history attributes its iconic emblem to Lulu's signature red lips, we have not identified the author or illustrator of this specific knitted/printed sweater motif, nor do we have a work-made-for-hire or assignment document for it. Could you please confirm if you are the rights holder for this specific artwork as it appears on the sweater, and if so, provide guidance on its current ownership?

Please confirm if you are able to grant these rights, any associated fees, and any restrictions that may apply. We are requesting an artwork reproduction release.
